newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: IRA rules out truce, N.Ireland tension builds.
newsitem.headline: IRA rules out truce, N.Ireland tension builds.

text.p: The IRA was reported on Friday to have ruled out any new truce to its war against London's rule until after a British election in the hope that a new government will give its Sinn Fein political wing a seat at peace talks.

A source close to the Irish Republican Army leadership told Dublin journalists that British Prime Minister John Major's refusal to ease terms for Sinn Fein's entry to the talks ruled out any immediate new IRA ceasefire.
The statement was made on the eve of the first anniversary of the IRA bombing of London's Canary Wharf business complex which ended the guerrillas' unprecedented 17-month truce.
"At the present there is no sign of a meaningful move from the British and in that event there is no immediate sign of a ceasefire," the source told British and Irish journalists.
Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, told BBC radio that he was "heartened" by the fact that the IRA statement said the guerrillas wanted to see a negotiated settlement.
But he said it would require a British leader of the stature of former South African President F.W. de Klerk to find a solution to Europe's longest guerrilla war.

The IRA abandoned the truce accusing Britain of blocking Sinn Fein's entry to the talks by insisting that progress be made on dismantling the guerrillas' armoury, which includes Semtex plastic explosive and sophisticated assault weaponry.

The London government says the Canary Wharf bombing, which killed two people, proved the IRA's truce was a tactical ploy, arguing that the guerrillas will continue to wage war if they do not get what they want at the negotiating table.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, told reporters that Sinn Fein would only get a ticket to talks if it abandoned its 27-year war for good.

He said current talks, grouping pro-British Protestant Unionist parties and the pro-Irish Catholic-backed SDLP, were made more difficult by continuing IRA violence, which has taken place almost every other day in Northern Ireland this year.
"Nobody can, by violence, insist upon having a place at that table in this, a democracy." Mayhew told reporters after late-night London talks with Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring.

Spring raised the Irish government's concern about a planned march on Saturday night by Northern Ireland Protestant activists to a Catholic church at Harryville, near Ballymena, which has been a target for Protestant protest for months.

"We raised concerns over what has been happening over many months in Harryville. I think it is fair to say that protests and pickets outside places of worship are unacceptable in any community in Northern Ireland," Spring told reporters.

Protestants say they will maintain their protest until Catholics in the nearby village of Dunloy drop their objections to marches by the Protestant Orange Order, which parades its British loyalty across the province from March until October.

The so-called "marching season" inflamed communal passions last year and caused the worst civil unrest in the province for years after police banned, then allowed, an Orange Order march through a Catholic street in the southern town of Portadown.
Spring said he was disappointed that Britain had failed to implement in full the recommendations of an independent commission on Northern Ireland's Protestant marches.
They said the commission should have the power to ban such parades, a power which the Northern Ireland police now has.
